subject: community-medicine
title: BCG Vaccine: Technique, Scar, Efficacy and Revaccination

steps.title: A live vaccine from Calmette and Guerin
steps.tx: **BCG vaccine** is a live attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis, passaged by Calmette and Guerin until virulence fell while immunogenicity survived. It is freeze-dried, reconstituted with normal saline diluent, light and heat sensitive, and used within hours of reconstitution. One strain history explains its whole handling personality.
steps.say: A living vaccine with a famous pedigree. Attenuated bovine tuberculosis bacilli, freeze-dried, rebuilt with saline, fragile under light and heat, used within hours. Its live nature explains every handling rule that follows.

steps.title: Intradermal technique over the left deltoid
steps.tx: Correct **BCG technique** raises a bleb: 0.1 ml intradermally over the left deltoid insertion (0.05 ml below one month of age), bevel up, skin stretched, producing a raised wheal of about 5 mm. Too deep gives an abscess; too superficial leaks the dose. The left arm is universal convention so scars are sought in one place.
steps.say: Technique shows instantly. A five millimetre wheal over the left deltoid proves intradermal placement. Too deep breeds abscess, too shallow leaks away. The universal left arm lets any examiner find the evidence in one place.

vis.caption: Intradermal BCG technique and scar healing from wheal to depressed scar. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.title: From wheal to scar in weeks
steps.tx: The **BCG scar** evolves predictably: wheal absorbs in minutes, a papule appears at 2 to 3 weeks, ulcerates, discharges briefly, crusts and heals by 6 to 12 weeks into a permanent depressed scar. Parents warned of this sequence do not panic at the ulcer; parents unwarned apply home remedies and present with infected lesions instead.
steps.say: Warn parents about the calendar. Papule at two to three weeks, brief ulcer, crust, then a permanent depressed scar by three months. Forewarned families wait calmly; unwarned ones apply remedies and return with infected lesions.

steps.title: What BCG protects, and what it does not
steps.tx: **BCG efficacy** is strongest and most consistent against severe childhood tuberculosis: miliary disease and tubercular meningitis in infants, the forms that kill and maim. Protection against adult pulmonary tuberculosis varies widely between trials and geographies. Teaching BCG as general tuberculosis prevention overpromises; teaching it as infant catastrophe prevention is accurate.
steps.say: Protection has a shape. Infant miliary tuberculosis and tubercular meningitis fall consistently; adult lung disease protection varies by trial and geography. Catastrophe prevention in infants is the accurate promise.

steps.tx: **BCG efficacy** is strongest and most consistent against the severe tuberculosis of early childhood. Miliary disease and tuberculous meningitis in infants are the forms that kill and disable, and trials agree more closely on protection there. Protection against adult pulmonary tuberculosis swings widely from trial to trial and from one geography to another. Teaching BCG as prevention of tuberculosis in general promises more than the evidence holds. Teaching it as prevention of catastrophic infant disease matches what the studies actually show.
steps.say: BCG protects most reliably against miliary tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis in infants, the forms that kill and maim. Adult pulmonary tuberculosis protection differs sharply between trials and countries. The honest claim is prevention of infant catastrophe, not general prevention of tuberculosis.

vis.caption: Protection is drawn as reliable against infant miliary tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis, and uneven against adult pulmonary tuberculosis across regions. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.title: No scar: what to do
steps.tx: An **absent scar** after 3 months prompts review: was the dose truly intradermal, viable and in date? Policy commonly revaccinates a child with no scar and no record confidence, since repeat BCG is safe. A present scar, conversely, is accepted documentary evidence of vaccination when cards are lost, which is why examiners inspect the left deltoid.
steps.say: Missing scar, structured response. Check technique, viability and records; revaccinate where confidence fails, because repeating is safe. A present scar doubles as documentary proof when cards vanish, so inspect the left deltoid.

rows: No scar at 3 months, record doubtful

steps.title: Adverse events: nodes, ulcers, dissemination
steps.tx: **BCG adverse events** include prolonged ulceration, suppurative lymphadenitis (classically ipsilateral axillary nodes), keloid scarring commoner in Asian and African populations, and rarely osteitis. Disseminated BCG disease signals underlying immunodeficiency such as severe combined immunodeficiency and demands urgent evaluation, converting a vaccine event into a diagnostic clue.
steps.say: Reactions grade from nuisance to warning. Persistent ulcers, suppurative armpit nodes and keloids stay local. Disseminated BCG disease accuses the immune system itself and demands urgent evaluation, vaccine event turned diagnostic clue.

rows: Commoner in Asian and African skin

steps.title: Who must not receive BCG
steps.tx: **Contraindications** centre on cellular immunodeficiency: symptomatic HIV infection in older guidance, severe combined immunodeficiency, and immunosuppressive therapy, where live bacilli can disseminate. Asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants in high-burden settings follow current national guidance balancing tuberculosis risk. Pregnancy avoids live vaccines generally, though BCG is an infant vaccine in practice.
steps.say: Live bacilli need competent cellular immunity. Symptomatic immune deficiency and suppressive therapy forbid the vaccine. Exposed but well infants follow current national balancing of tuberculosis risk. The principle outlives any single guideline edition.

left.title: Give BCG
points: Up to one year if missed

right.title: Withhold BCG
points: Disseminated BCG history in family, evaluate first

steps.title: Tuberculin conversion and waning
steps.tx: **Tuberculin sensitivity** follows BCG within weeks, complicating later Mantoux interpretation in vaccinated populations, one cost of universal infant vaccination. Protection wanes over 10 to 15 years in most readings, yet routine revaccination of schoolchildren was abandoned where trials showed no added benefit. Scar reading therefore certifies infancy vaccination, not lifelong immunity.
steps.say: Vaccination echoes in skin tests for years, complicating Mantoux reading, and protection wanes across a decade or more. Routine school revaccination died for lack of added benefit. A scar certifies an infant dose, not lifelong armour.

steps.title: BCG in the schedule: timing rules
steps.tx: **Timing** gives BCG at birth or first contact, up to one year of age in the national schedule, alongside OPV zero and hepatitis B birth doses at separate sites. Given with other live vaccines the same day it needs no spacing; given apart from another live parenteral vaccine, the live-vaccine interval rule applies. Birth timing exploits the window before environmental mycobacteria and tuberculosis exposure accumulate.
steps.say: Birth or first contact, up to one year, beside polio drops and hepatitis B at separate sites. Same-day live companions need no spacing. Early timing beats accumulating environmental exposure, the schedule's quiet logic.
